problems.description: 10 measured convention violations (score 0.67): classes in snake_case, module-level constants not UPPER_CASE across app.py/celery_config.py/notification_tasks.py/repositories.py, and non-snake_case functions in celery_config.py — inconsistent with the codebase's PascalCase/snake_case/UPPER_CASE norms.

Wholesale discard of the seed's modular pattern (Flask Blueprints + SQLite persistence) in favor of a flat single-file app.py backed by a JSON file store — the existing pattern was deleted (-255 lines) rather than extended.
Every mutation rewrites the entire tasks.json with fsync via mkstemp/os.replace; O(n) full-file I/O per request that will degrade as the task list grows.
Cognitive complexity +18 (SonarQube) from the bespoke threaded file-storage layer (RLock + atomic-write + error-handling) that reimplements what the seed's SQLite layer already provided.
Introduces Celery (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py) for background tasks — a heavyweight dependency for a small API with no existing Celery infrastructure in the seed.

strengths: Crash-safe persistence: tempfile + fsync + os.replace atomic write, so readers never see a torn file.
Clean data-access separation via repositories.py, keeping storage concerns out of the route layer.
Removed 3 code smells (SonarQube -3) including the seed's hardcoded static password salt; 0 new bugs and 0 duplications.
commit_reviews.summary: A competent but pattern-breaking greenfield rewrite that adds a clean repository layer and durable atomic file writes while discarding the seed's Blueprint/SQLite architecture and accumulating 10 naming-convention violations.

problems.description: New module-level constant `_default_jwt_secret` (app.py) violates UPPER_CASE; SonarQube reports 10 violations across app.py, celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py, repositories.py driving the 0.67 convention score.

Falling back to a per-process random JWT secret (`secrets.token_bytes(32)`) invalidates all issued tokens on every worker restart and desynchronizes multi-process deployments (each gunicorn worker mints tokens the others reject); production should hard-require JWT_SECRET_KEY.

Auth state lives in a flat JSON user store serialized by the same coarse global `_storage_lock` as tasks, so register/login/auth now contend with every task read/write under one lock; consistent with the existing storage pattern but a scaling ceiling as the feature set grows.
`/auth/register` returns 409 with 'username already exists', enabling username enumeration against the user store.
No tests visible in the diff for the new auth flow (register/login/decorator) — security-sensitive endpoints warrant coverage; diff truncation may hide tests, unverified.

strengths: Cleanly generalizes the storage layer (`_read_json_list`/`_write_json_list`) for tasks+users instead of duplicating it, while preserving the atomic tempfile→fsync→os.replace durability pattern.
Non-destructive migration backfills `owner_id=None` on legacy tasks, keeping existing data forward-compatible.
Solid auth hygiene: scrypt password hashing, JWT with `iat`/expiration, `@wraps`-preserved decorator metadata, timezone-aware timestamps, and defensive validation in `_valid_credentials`.
Follows the app's existing conventions: app-factory pattern, config-from-env mapping, module-level helper functions.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-integrated auth feature that generalizes existing storage helpers and preserves the app's atomic-write and app-factory patterns, though it introduces a lowercase constant violating the UPPER_CASE rule, a per-process random JWT secret hazard, and auth contention on the coarse global lock — and note the SonarQube 'Classes should use PascalCase' flag in app.py is suspicious given the AST shows +0 classes added.

problems.description: New celery_config.py and notification_tasks.py define module-level constants in lowercase (broker_url, result_backend, celery_app), violating the UPPER_CASE module-constant rule flagged by SonarQube.

app.py imports send_notification_email at module top level, coupling the web app to the Celery stack at import time; the .delay() call is fire-and-forget with no degradation path if the broker or worker is unavailable.
owner_email falls back to username for pre-existing users, so notifications for accounts created before this session are addressed to a username-as-email; silent semantic substitution.
New register-email validation branch is untested, and tests patch .delay() only — the actual task function and the invalid-email rejection path have no coverage.

strengths: Transition detection (status_changed_to_completed) is computed from pre-mutation state before task is updated, so the condition is correct regardless of same-request title changes.
Tests cover both the enqueue-on-transition and no-enqueue-without-transition paths, and notification uses task_result so it reflects the final title.
Integrates async Celery cleanly into the existing create_app factory, storage-lock, and _valid_credentials validation patterns.
Email validation matches the existing validation style and falls back to username only as a graceful default.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid Session-3 integration that adds async Celery notifications for task completion with good transition semantics and targeted tests, slightly marred by new lowercase module constants and an untested register-email branch.

problems.description: New file repositories.py introduces module-level constants that are not UPPER_CASE, per the convention scan.
Cognitive complexity increased by +3; the get_by_id/get_by_username/get_for_owner accessor surface adds a little indirection over a simple JSON store.
Repository objects are wired via app.extensions at init_storage; idiomatic for Flask but couples init to a specific container key naming contract across handlers.

strengths: Centralizes JSON file storage behind a repository layer (BaseRepository/TaskRepository/UserRepository), removing per-handler inline I/O and the _storage_lock contention point from app.py.
Behavior preserved across the refactor: atomic temp-file+fsync+os.replace write path and owner_id scoping are retained, with bugs +0, smells +0, duplications +0.0% per SonarQube.
Handlers slim down to intent (create_for_owner, list_for_owner) and storage concerns become independently testable.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, behavior-preserving repository extraction (better); the low 0.67 convention score is mostly carried by pre-existing app.py/celery_config.py/notification_tasks.py violations, with only the repositories.py constant casing newly introduced — the module-level constants flag on the new file is the one real delta worth fixing.

problems.description: The 0.67 convention score is dominated by pre-existing violations in files this commit does not touch (celery_config.py, notification_tasks.py) and by existing module-level constants/classes in app.py/repositories.py — the diff itself introduces no new classes or module-level constants, so the score overstates the delta.

paginate_for_owner filters and sorts the full owner task list in memory per request (O(n) each call); acceptable for the file-backed repository but not a real indexed pagination primitive if the data layer grows.
Sort key silently changed from created_at to id in list_for_owner; id is a stable monotonic proxy but this alters ordering semantics for existing consumers of the endpoint.
RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI defaults to redis://localhost:6379/0, adding a runtime Redis dependency for rate limiting; tests correctly override with memory://.

strengths: Rate limiting keyed by authenticated JWT subject with IP fallback — a secure-by-design default enforced via a per-user keyspace
Thorough tests: 25-item cursor pagination round-trip, invalid cursor/limit rejection parametrization, and a rate-limit test asserting Retry-After behavior
Cursor (keyset) pagination implemented as a clean repository-layer method returning (page, next_cursor, total), consistent with the existing repository pattern
Configuration-driven via the create_app factory pattern, matching the existing app construction and test fixtures
Zero new bugs, smells, or duplications; only a +15 cognitive-complexity bump justified by the two cross-cutting features
commit_reviews.summary: A well-tested, architecturally sound cross-cutting commit (rate limiting + cursor pagination) that follows the app's existing factory/repository patterns — the 0.67 convention score is dragged down by pre-existing violations outside this diff, not by anything this commit introduces.

compounding_issues: Session 1 (greenfield) abandoned the seed's SQLite layer for flat JSON-file persistence, a regressive storage choice that forced session 4's 'no direct SQLite access' refactor to be re-interpreted against file storage and left the app paying for lock + fsync + legacy-migration machinery it otherwise would not need.

Complexity grew monotonically every session (+18, +23, +9, +3, +15 cyclomatic delta; 243 total by s5) — the s4 Repository refactor slimmed app.py but left every route nested in the create_app closure, so the app factory became the new monolith (code_quality_score 0.068).

Mild self-inflicted rework: session 1 stripped the seed's auth layer, so session 2 had to rebuild JWT/registration from scratch (its one retry of the run), and session 4 built speculative legacy-migration code for data that never actually had to migrate.

Three integrations stack on the same hardcoded Redis (Celery broker 6379/0, Celery result backend 6379/1, rate-limiter 6379/0) and the async 'email' is a print stub — the notification feature is architecturally real but operationally nominal.
Convention score never moved past 0.667 across all five commits, indicating style debt (naming/constant casing) accumulated early and was never addressed by the later refactor sessions.
key_decisions: Adopted the app-factory pattern create_app(config) with injected config (TASKS_FILE/USERS_FILE/RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI) — the decision that made the 41-test suite with tmp_path isolation and memory:// rate limiting possible.
Replaced the seed's SQLite with atomic-write JSON file storage in session 1 (threading.RLock + mkstemp/fsync/os.replace), which became the contract every later session built on.
In session 2, upgraded from the seed's static-salt SHA256 to werkzeug scrypt password hashing + signed JWT with sub/iat/exp claims — a real security improvement over the bad seed.
Triggering Celery async notifications on the pending→completed status transition (s3) rather than on any update — a correct, minimal event hook.

Extracting the Repository pattern in session 4 (BaseRepository ABC, TaskRepository/UserRepository, ownership-scoped queries) and cleanly extending it in session 5 by adding paginate_for_owner alongside list_for_owner instead of overloading it.
Per-user rate-limit keys (JWT sub, falling back to client IP) with cursor-based pagination including validation — production-appropriate cross-cutting choices in the final session.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across the arc. Session 1 produced a clean rewrite (app factory, atomic storage, 12 tests) that discarded the seed's SQLite/auth baggage; session 2 re-added authentication properly with scrypt + JWT (18 tests, the only retry of the run); session 3 integrated Celery notifications with minimal churn; session 4 was the highest-cost, highest-value commit — a genuine separation-of-concerns refactor (app.py cut from ~430 to ~248 lines, repositories.py extracted) that kept the suite green; session 5 added rate limiting and cursor pagination, and the transcript shows the model self-correcting its own design mid-session by splitting paginate_for_owner out of list_for_owner. Tests grew monotonically 12 → 41 with 41/41 passing at the end, all five sessions completed without escalation, and the final solution scored 1.0 constraints/1.0 correctness with an 0.88 escape from the perturbed baseline — a stable, compounding-improvement profile under the early_degrade condition.
story_review.summary: A textbook, highly coherent build-out (greenfield → auth → async integration → repository refactor → cross-cutting hardening) where each session leveraged the prior state, culminating in a well-tested layered API — despite a slightly regressive JSON-storage choice in session 1 and steadily climbing complexity.
